prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Annual Business Survey (ABS)
Description: The Annual Business Survey (ABS) measures business owner demographics, research and development (R&D), innovation, and other topics of interest among businesses in the United States. The Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey was integrated into the ABS in 2025. The ABS is a joint statistical project between the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) within the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and the U.S. Census Bureau.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Annual Business Survey (ABS)
Description: The Annual Business Survey (ABS) measures business owner demographics, research and development (R&D), innovation, and other topics of interest among businesses in the United States. The Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey was integrated into the ABS in 2025. The ABS is a joint statistical project between the National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) within the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) and the U.S. Census Bureau.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

I'll research this dataset comprehensively, starting with several parallel searches.I have a solid foundation. Now let me dig deeper into the legal authority, data access channels, users, and the 2025 BERD integration details.I have strong coverage of history, authority, and users. Let me fill remaining gaps: data access channels, confidentiality/microdata access, and the latest releases.I've gathered comprehensive information from the Census Bureau, NCSES/NSF, the Federal Register, and secondary sources. Here is the full report.

---

# The Annual Business Survey (ABS): A Comprehensive Research Report

## 1. Verification of the Provided Description

Your description is **substantially accurate**, with two clarifications worth noting:

1. **"The BERD Survey was integrated into the ABS in 2025"** — This is correct as to *when the decision was made and announced*, but the first integrated fielding is slightly later. The Census Bureau formally announced the combination in 2025 (Federal Register notices and an "Important Change" banner on census.gov); the Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey was discontinued **after the 2024 survey year**; and the first ABS collection to carry the former BERD content is the collection that begins in **May 2026**, which will be branded **"ABS Reference Year 2025."** Along with the merger, the survey changed its naming convention from *collection year* to *data reference year*.

2. **Division of labor:** The ABS is conducted by the Census Bureau and co-sponsored by NCSES. The two agencies split dissemination: the **Census Bureau releases the business/owner demographic data** (via data.census.gov and the Census API), while **NCSES releases the R&D, innovation, and technology data** (via ncses.nsf.gov).

## 2. Publisher and Governance

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Conducting agency** | U.S. Census Bureau (U.S. Department of Commerce) |
| **Co-sponsor / statistical partner** | National Center for Science and Engineering Statistics (NCSES) within the U.S. National Science Foundation |
| **OMB control number** | 0607-1004 (first approved March 7, 2018) |
| **Form numbers** | ABS-1, ABS-2 (worksheets); now ABS-1 |
| **Frequency** | Annual |
| **Status** | Active (as of 2026) |
| **Type** | Mandatory, sample survey of employer businesses |

The Census Bureau collects, processes, and tabulates the data "in accordance with a joint project agreement" between the two agencies. OMB's June 2025 terms of clearance codified the partnership: the Census Bureau must transmit all collected data to NCSES upon request and must obtain NCSES's written approval before revising the collection — an unusual arrangement reflecting the dual-agency stake in the data.

## 3. Legal Authority and Mandate

- **Title 13, U.S. Code, Sections 8(b), 131, and 182** — the Census Bureau's core economic-statistics authorities.
- **Title 42, U.S. Code, Sections 1861–76 (National Science Foundation Act of 1950, as amended)** — NCSES's authority to collect statistics on the science and engineering enterprise.
- **Title 13, Section 224** — makes response **mandatory**; businesses that fail to respond are subject to penalties.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act (44 U.S.C. ch. 45)** — each year's rotating content and periodic re-clearance of core content go through the OMB ICR process with 60-/30-day Federal Register comment periods. The core questions are cleared every three years (last cleared 2024).
- The Census Bureau's periodic "Current Mandatory Business Surveys" Federal Register notices (e.g., 90 FR, April 4, 2025; September 2026) formally determine that ABS data "are needed to aid the efficient performance of essential governmental functions" and "are not publicly available from nongovernmental or other governmental sources."
- Under the **Foundations for Evidence-Based Policymaking Act of 2018** (per OMB's 2025 terms of clearance), ABS data assets must be cataloged in the agency's comprehensive data inventory.

## 4. History and Lineage

The ABS, first fielded for **reference year 2017** (initial mailout June 2018), is a consolidation of multiple long-running federal statistical collections. Understanding its predecessors is essential for time-series work:

**Demographic/entrepreneurship lineage:**
- **Survey of Business Owners (SBO)** — conducted as part of the Economic Census every five years **since 1972** (with antecedents in the 1969 Survey of Minority-Owned Business Enterprises). Collected owner sex, ethnicity, race, and veteran status. The ABS replaced the SBO *for employer businesses* starting with reference year 2017; nonemployer coverage moved to the separate **Nonemployer Statistics by Demographics (NES-D)** program.
- **Annual Survey of Entrepreneurs (ASE)** — conducted for reference years 2014–2016 as an SBO supplement; absorbed into the ABS.
- **Characteristics of Business Owners (CBO) Survey** — an earlier related survey (funded in part by MBDA and SBA through 1992).

**R&D/innovation lineage (NCSES-sponsored, collected by Census):**
- **Survey of Industrial Research and Development (SIRD)** — data years **1953–2007**. NCSES has cosponsored an annual business R&D survey since 1953.
- **Business R&D and Innovation Survey (BRDIS)** — 2008–2016.
- **Business Research and Development Survey (BRDS)** — 2017–2018 (renamed after innovation content moved to the ABS).
- **Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey** — 2019 through the 2024 survey year, when it was discontinued and folded into the ABS.
- **Business R&D and Innovation for Microbusinesses (BRDI-M)** — first fielded 2016; absorbed into the ABS from the start.

**Key design rationale** (consistent across every Federal Register notice since 2017): combine Census Bureau firm-level collections to **reduce respondent burden, increase data quality, reduce operational costs, and operate more efficiently**, while creating an *adaptive* survey that rotates topical modules annually. The National Academies' 2017 panel report (*Integrating Federal Statistics on Business and Industrial R&D*, Ch. 8) describes the ABS as the response to longstanding calls for an integrated annual business survey system.

**The 2025–2026 BERD integration:** Per the February 2026 Federal Register notice, "Content previously collected on the Business Enterprise Research and Development (BERD) Survey will now be collected as part of the Annual Business Survey. The BERD survey will no longer be fielded independently." Integrating the instruments necessitated question changes that were tested with target populations, developed collaboratively by Census and NCSES. Critically, this ends the historical split in which the ABS collected R&D only from **microbusinesses (1–9 employees)** while BERD sampled ~45,000 companies with **10+ employees** — the unified ABS now spans the full employer size range, with an explicit "skip" design (firms reporting $0 R&D skip the R&D section).

## 5. What the ABS Measures

- **Business/owner demographics:** sex, ethnicity, race, and veteran status of up to four majority owners; owner age, education, and other characteristics; firm counts, receipts, payroll, and employment by owner class.
- **R&D (formerly split between ABS and BERD):** R&D performance and expenditure, total and R&D employment, sources of R&D funding, type of R&D work (basic research, applied research, development), R&D costs (salaries, etc.), R&D capital expenditures, tax credits for research activities, and (from nonprofits) research activities.
- **Innovation:** product innovation (new-to-market vs. new-to-business), business-process innovation — collected on a three-year reference period (e.g., 2021–23 for the 2024 cycle).
- **Technology, intellectual property, and technology transfer.**
- **Rotating/adaptive modules by year:** financing practices, COVID-19 pandemic effects, management practices, domestic/foreign transactions, critical and emerging technologies, and similar topical content.
- **Nonprofit module:** starting with the 2025 ABS, ~8,000 nonprofit organizations (excluding universities) in R&D-performing industries are sampled for research activities only — not owner demographics.

## 6. Universe, Sample, and Methodology

- **Universe:** all domestic, nonfarm, for-profit employer businesses filing IRS tax forms (proprietorships, partnerships, corporations) with receipts of $1,000 or more — roughly **5.6 million employer businesses** — plus the nonprofit supplement.
- **Sample sizes (a moving target, important for comparability):**
  - 2017 and every fifth year thereafter: **~850,000** employer businesses (2023 ABS, reference year 2022, was the last 850k cycle) — large enough for detailed statistics by 2–6-digit NAICS, geography down to county and economic place, and detailed race groups (e.g., Chinese, Filipino, Japanese, Samoan).
  - Non-quinqennial years: ~300,000 (2024 ABS: 330,000), yielding summary-level estimates at 3-digit NAICS and national/state/MSA levels.
  - **2025 ABS: reduced to ~230,000**, with sampling changes to reduce repeat selection of the same firms, removal of Telephone Follow-Up, and removal of chronic nonresponders from mailout.
- **Burden:** 2017: 850,000 respondents × 52 min = 735,934 hours. 2025: 230,000 × 29 min = 112,367 hours — a deliberate ~85% reduction in respondent burden.
- **Design:** systematic stratified sampling with simple random sampling within strata; stratified by state, industry, and one of **eight demographic sampling frames** (American Indian/Alaska Native; Asian; Black; Hispanic; Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander; non-Hispanic White men; publicly owned; women). Firms are classified into frames using administrative record imputation — owners identified via IRS K-1 filings and the Business Register, then matched through a Protected Identification Key to the 2000/2010 Decennial Censuses, the ACS (2005–22), and SSA's Numident file for race/ethnicity/sex and country of birth. Large firms and known R&D performers are selected with certainty.
- **Key definitions:** ownership = **51%+ of stock or equity**; separate tabulations exist for 50/50 equally-owned firms; "minority-owned" = any race/ethnicity combination other than non-Hispanic White.
- **Mode:** electronic-only, web-based questionnaire; annual mailout typically in July (formerly February for BERD); responses due in the fall.
- **Data sources combined:** survey responses + Economic Census data + administrative records.

## 7. Data Products and Access Channels

**From the Census Bureau (demographic/business characteristics):**
- **data.census.gov** — table search and download.
- **Census API** (`api.census.gov`, ABS datasets) — four main table suites: **Company Summary**; **Characteristics of Businesses**; **Characteristics of Business Owners**; and the **Module Business Characteristics** (introduced 2021; covers technology use, financing practices, pandemic effects; urban/rural classification available for 2021–2024).
- Excel/CSV downloadable tables and technical documentation (methodology, sampling, source-and-accuracy statements, questionnaires) at census.gov/programs-surveys/abs.html.

**From NCSES (R&D, innovation, technology):**
- NCSES-ABS survey pages by cycle (ncses.nsf.gov/surveys/annual-business-survey), with annual detailed data tables (e.g., **NSF 26-321**, *Annual Business Survey: 2024 (Data Year 2023)*) and survey descriptions (e.g., **NCSES 26-007**).
- NCSES **Data Explorer, Chart Builder, and Table Builder** tools at ncsesdata.nsf.gov.
- Former BERD-series data (10+ employee R&D: SIRD 1953–2007, BRDIS 2008–2016, BRDS 2017–2018, BERD 2019–2025) consolidated on the NCSES-BERD data page.
- **Public-use files** and a **Restricted-Use Data Licensing** program via NCSES; confidential microdata are also accessible to approved researchers through the **Federal Statistical Research Data Centers (FSRDCs)** under Title 13 confidentiality protections — the standard route for firm-level linked analysis.

**Citation/persistence notes for preservationists:** NCSES publications carry persistent product IDs (e.g., NSF 26-321, NCSES 26-007); Census tables are versioned by survey year on data.census.gov; the OMB ICR record (0607-1004) and Federal Register notices (2017-16605, 2017-23041, 2017-28021, 2018-12356, 2023-01147, 2025-05463, 2026-02453, and the annual "Current Mandatory Business Surveys" notices) form a complete paper trail of the collection's legal and content history. The change from collection-year to reference-year naming (2026) is a metadata hazard for cataloging: "2024 ABS" (collection) = "reference year 2023" = NCSES product "ABS 2024."

## 8. Users and Uses

**Federal government:**
- **Small Business Administration (SBA)** and **Minority Business Development Agency (MBDA)** — assess business assistance needs and allocate program resources; MBDA and SBA part-funded predecessor surveys (e.g., CBO through 1992).
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA)** — ABS R&D estimates feed the national accounts; R&D estimates from the ABS "are used as part of the calculations for investment in quarterly GDP."
- **National Science Board** — the biennial *Science and Engineering Indicators* report.
- **National Women's Business Council** — state-of-women's-business-ownership assessments.
- Local government commissions on small/disadvantaged businesses — procurement practices and program evaluation.

**International/statistical system:** OECD periodic publications and international R&D comparisons (including with the European Union); NCSES's *National Patterns of R&D Resources*; nonprofit-module users include the Science Philanthropy Alliance, the Association of Independent Research Institutes, and the Health Research Alliance.

**Private sector, academia, civil society:** industry organization leaders; corporate planners comparing R&D costs across industries and locating R&D geographically; economic and social analysts; consultants tracking long-term demographic shifts; journalists; individual business owners benchmarking operations, market share, and growth prospects; state data centers (e.g., NY DOL uses ABS in workforce analysis).

## 9. Benefits to the Public

- **The only comprehensive national source of business ownership by owner demographics.** Combined with NES-D, the ABS provides the only detailed statistics on *all* U.S. businesses by owner sex, ethnicity, race, and veteran status — foundational for civil-rights and economic-equity analysis. (Example finding, 2021 ABS/data year 2020: 19.9% of employer businesses were minority-owned; 5.6% veteran-owned; 21.4% women-owned.)
- **Measurement of ~75% of total U.S. R&D.** R&D data from for-profit businesses and sampled nonprofits account for nearly three-quarters of U.S. R&D expenditures each year — the basis for R&D/GDP measures, fed into quarterly GDP, and indispensable for science and competitiveness policy.
- **Reduced respondent burden and taxpayer cost** — the founding rationale, achieved by consolidating five predecessor collections into one, and dramatically advanced by the 2025 BERD merger and sample reduction.
- **Program accountability:** enables the public to evaluate whether SBA/MBDA/federal procurement programs actually reach minority-, women-, and veteran-owned firms.
- **International comparability** of U.S. innovation performance (OECD Frascati-aligned measures).
- **Adaptive relevance:** rotating modules let the survey respond quickly to emerging issues (pandemic effects, management practices, emerging technologies).

## 10. Caveats, Comparability Issues, and Watch Items

- **Sample-size breaks:** the 850k quinqennial vs. ~300k/230k annual cycles mean **geographic and industry detail varies sharply by year** — county- and 6-digit-NAICS-level detail only exists in the big-cycle years. Analysts must check which cycle they are using.
- **Series breaks:** the ABS is *not* strictly comparable to the SBO/ASE/BRDIS/BERD series it replaced (different universes, definitions, modes). The 2025–26 BERD integration introduces new question wording (tested, but changed), and 2017 was itself a break year.
- **Content removals in the 2025 ABS** (per the March 31, 2025 Federal Register notice): questions on **working from home, sexual orientation and gender identity of owners, business collaboration (e.g., with universities), and management practices** were dropped — a significant loss for researchers studying LGBTQ business ownership. (Management practices were slated to return as 2026 ABS variable content.)
- **Naming change:** collection-year → reference-year branding beginning with the May 2026 collection ("ABS Reference Year 2025").
- **Employer-only universe** (plus the recent nonprofit supplement): the ABS does not cover nonemployers — use NES-D for those.
- **Release lag:** the R&D/innovation products lag considerably (the 2024 cycle / data year 2023 NCSES tables were released August 17, 2026 — a ~2.7-year lag); Census demographic tables release on a different schedule. Featured finding from the latest release: **U.S. microbusinesses performed $5.9 billion of R&D in 2023** (NSF 26-324).
- **Sibling-survey confusion:** the Annual Integrated Economic Survey (AIES), also mandatory and consolidating other economic collections, does *not* collect the detailed R&D, innovation, or owner-demographic content of the ABS — a distinction the agencies' FAQ explicitly draws.

## 11. Key Primary Sources

- Census ABS program page: census.gov/programs-surveys/abs.html (and /about, /about/faq, /data, /technical-documentation/methodology)
- Census ABS API datasets: census.gov/data/developers/data-sets/abs.html
- NCSES ABS survey pages: ncses.nsf.gov/surveys/annual-business-survey (2021–2024 cycles online)
- BERD discontinuation notice: census.gov/programs-surveys/brds.html
- Federal Register: 2017-16605; 2017-23041; 2017-28021; 2018-12356; 2023-01147 (88 FR 3968, rich "Needs and Uses" statement); 2025-05463; 2025-05843; 2026-02453; 2026-18176
- OMB ICR record 0607-1004 (202503-0607-003, approved with change June 17, 2025 — includes the NCSES data-transmission and approval terms)
- NCSES publications: NCSES 26-007 (survey description), NSF 26-321 (data tables), NSF 26-324 (microbusiness R&D analysis)
- National Academies (2017), *Integrating Federal Statistics on Business and Industrial R&D*, Ch. 8

---

**Bottom line:** The ABS is one of the federal statistical system's most significant consolidations — merging a 50+ year Census Bureau business-demographics tradition (SBO, since 1972) with NCSES's 70+ year business-R&D measurement program (SIRD, since 1953) — and, with the 2025 BERD integration, it is now the single mandatory annual instrument through which the U.S. measures both *who owns American businesses* and *how much they invest in research and innovation*. ### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

## 1. Historical Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- All prior-cycle ABS products remain posted and accessible: Census ABS methodology pages for 2018–2024, the ABS API datasets (2017–2023 data years), and NCSES survey pages for the 2021–2024 cycles are all live, with the newest release (NSF 26-321, data year 2023) published August 2026. The Census FAQ explicitly states "Prior ABS data releases will not have the year and name change" accompanying the 2026 renaming.
- The discontinued BERD Survey's historical series (SIRD 1953–2007 through BERD 2024) remains consolidated and available on the NCSES-BERD data page.
- The ABS does **not** appear on the essentialdata.us / dataindex.us terminations tracker as a terminated dataset or removed dataset.
- **Caveat:** In late January–February 2025, thousands of Census Bureau webpages (research/methodology, data stewardship, survey documentation) were taken down in the scramble to comply with Executive Order 14168, and several LGBTQ-data pages went dark. NPR reported it remains unclear whether any data tables were permanently deleted; most content was later restored. Data.census.gov itself stayed online throughout. ABS-specific historical files show no documented permanent loss.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** No ABS data file from a prior cycle has been documented as removed, though the January 2025 Census-wide purge and the lack of agency transparency about what was scrubbed warrant ongoing verification by preservationists (a point made explicitly by NPR and the Boston Globe reporting).

## 2. Future Data Availability

**Evidence:**
- Collection is active and continuing: the 2025 ABS was fielded (mailout/response through fall 2025), and the integrated ABS/BERD collection mailed in **May 2026** ("ABS Reference Year 2025").
- The ICR is current: OMB 0607-1004 was renewed with change on June 17, 2025 (ICR 202503-0607-003) and again approved May 15, 2026 (ICR 202602-0607-001, expiration 5/31/2027). The September 2026 "Current Mandatory Business Surveys" notice formally re-determines the ABS as essential for 2026.
- The BERD merger is a consolidation, not a termination — R&D content continues under the ABS instrument, and the agencies frame it as increasing data quality.
- **Watch items:** The October 1–November 13, 2025 government shutdown forced rescheduling of economic data releases agency-wide and RIF notices (~100 staff) were issued during it; the mailout month shifted from the typical July to May 2026; and the 2025 mailout itself was subject to the sample redesign. No ABS publication deadline (there is no statutory deadline) has been reported as missed.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** The survey is fielding on schedule under an active ICR, with ongoing annual Federal Register re-authorization. The timing shift to May 2026 is an intended redesign, and shutdown-related disruption, while real, did not skip an ABS collection or publication.

## 3. Data Quality

**Evidence:**
- **Sample cut ~32%:** from 338,000 to 230,000 employer businesses/nonprofits for the 2025 ABS (Federal Register, 90 FR 14231, March 31, 2025; OMB ICR record), directly reducing the granularity available in non-quinqennial years (already limited to 3-digit NAICS/state/MSA).
- **Telephone Follow-Up eliminated** — explicitly "to reduce the type of contacts we have with respondents and increase cost savings" — a known risk to response rates and nonresponse bias.
- **Chronic nonresponders removed from mailout** and sampling changes reducing repeat selection — further implications for data quality and longitudinal comparability.
- **Content stripped:** questions on work from home, sexual orientation, gender identity, business collaboration, and management practices removed in 2025 (per the same Federal Register notice and the Census Project/MAP analyses).
- **Series breaks:** the BERD integration introduces new question wording and naming conventions, creating comparability discontinuities across the R&D time series (which itself already has 1953/2008/2017/2019 breaks).
- **Counterweight:** the BERD merger extends full R&D measurement to all employer size classes (previously microbusiness-only in ABS), an improvement in one dimension.

**Finding: High Risk.** The 2025 redesign combines a one-third sample reduction, elimination of a follow-up mode, removal of population coverage (chronic nonresponders), and deletion of content areas — documented reductions in granularity and (for SOGI topics) outright elimination — squarely meeting the "reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency" threshold. The agency's own justification (cost savings, burden reduction) confirms these are resource-driven, not purely methodological.

## 4. Statutory Context

**Evidence:**
- Authorizing statutes are explicitly named in the ICR: **13 U.S.C. 8(b), 131, 182** (Census) and **42 U.S.C. 1861–76** (NSF Act of 1950, as amended), plus the America COMPETES Reauthorization Act of 2010 (Pub. L. 111-358, §505).
- The Census Bureau's annual Federal Register determinations state the data "are needed to aid the efficient performance of essential governmental functions" and "are not publicly available from nongovernmental or other governmental sources" — an explicit no-substitute finding.
- The ABS is required for implementation of federal programs: BEA's national accounts (R&D feeds quarterly GDP), SBA/MBDA minority- and women-owned business program assessment, and the National Science Board's *Science and Engineering Indicators*. No alternative collection measures business ownership demographics or ~75% of U.S. R&D.
- **Caveat:** No statute mandates the ABS *by name* (unlike, e.g., the Economic Census under 13 U.S.C. 131); its specific content is determined administratively, which is what allowed the 2025 content removals to proceed via ICR rather than statute.

**Finding: No Known Issue.** Statutory authorization is explicitly named, what must be collected is clear (owner demographics under Title 13 authority; R&D statistics under the NSF Act), there are no substitute data collections, and the data are required for implementation of federal programs (GDP, SBA/MBDA programs). This satisfies the strongest rubric tier, with the minor caveat that the survey's specific topical content is not itself statutorily fixed.

## 5. Staffing and Funding

**Evidence:**
- **Census Bureau:** ~1,300–1,500 employees lost since January 2025 (deferred resignations, early retirements, ~100 RIF notices during the shutdown) — roughly 10–15% of the ~13,230-person workforce (AFGE Council 241; GovExec; Bloomberg Law; ASA). The FY26 President's Budget Request would cut current-surveys staffing further (5,896 FTEs, −2%; overall −9% from FY24) and cuts the current-surveys account ~14% in purchasing power (ASA, *The Nation's Data at Risk 2025*).
- **Leadership removed:** Director Robert Santos resigned under pressure in January 2025; career Deputy Director Ron Jarmin was replaced as acting director by political appointee George Cook in September 2025 (CBPP; AP). This meets the rubric's "leadership removed" trigger on its own.
- **NSF/NCSES:** NSF staffing reportedly reduced by one-third between January and July 2025; FY26 request cuts NSF FTEs 25.4%. NCSES's FY26 President's Budget Request is **$44 million, a 40% decrease** from the comparable FY24 level (ASA); NCSES's own leadership was reshuffled in the August 2025 NSF restructuring (Deputy Director Freyman reassigned to head SBE), and NCSES faces a proposed relocation. NSF is heavily reliant on contractors for survey operations, compounding risk.
- Mitigants: FY25 Census funding was flat (not cut) at $1.385B; the final FY26 CJS appropriations report includes supportive Senate language for NCSES and additional staffing.

**Finding: High Risk.** The rubric's High Risk threshold is met on multiple independent grounds: leadership removed at the conducting agency (Santos/Jarmin/Cook), staff losses in the 10–15% range at Census (Moderate on its own, but combined with leadership), a ~40% proposed budget cut at the co-sponsoring NCSES, and a one-third staffing reduction at parent agency NSF. The ABS's dual-agency structure means it is exposed to disruption at *either* Commerce or NSF.

## 6. Policy

**Evidence:**
- **Presidential Action-driven ICR change:** Executive Order 14168 ("Defending Women From Gender Ideology and Extremism," Jan. 20, 2025) directly drove the removal of sexual orientation and gender identity questions from the ABS, documented in the March 31, 2025 Federal Register notice implementing the 2025 redesign. The Williams Institute estimates 360 federal data collections were affected by EO 14168; the Census Project and MAP identify the ABS by name, noting the removal "eliminates the only nationally representative federal data source on LGBTQ-owned employer businesses."
- **Other administration-priority changes:** removal of work-from-home, business-collaboration, and management-practices questions; the sample reduction and TFU elimination framed in efficiency/burden-reduction terms consistent with DOGE-era priorities; the dataindex.us tracker counts the ABS ICR among "100s of Information Collections Influenced by Presidential Actions."
- Broader context: the January–February 2025 web purge of LGBTQ- and diversity-related content at Census (3,000+ pages removed, later mostly restored), and the administration-wide push to shrink the federal workforce that hit both parent agencies.
- Mitigants: the BERD merger and core demographic/R&D content continue; the survey was not terminated and its core mission (R&D, innovation, race/ethnicity/sex/veteran owner demographics) is intact; some removed content (management practices) was slated to return as 2026 variable content.

**Finding: High Risk.** This is a textbook match for the rubric's High Risk tier: a presidential-action-driven change to an information collection, plus other significant content changes made in accordance with Administration priorities. The changes were executed through the normal ICR process (with public comment), which is a procedural mitigant, but the substantive content losses are real, permanent for the affected topics, and attributable to Executive Order 14168.

---

## Summary of Risk Levels

| Category | Level | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|
| **Historical Data Availability** | No Known Issue | All prior-cycle ABS and predecessor-survey files remain accessible; no documented permanent loss (January 2025 Census-wide purge is a verification caveat, not a confirmed ABS loss) |
| **Future Data Availability** | No Known Issue | Collection active (2026 fielding underway), ICR renewed through 5/31/2027, annual Federal Register re-determination issued September 2026 |
| **Data Quality** | High Risk | ~32% sample cut, Telephone Follow-Up eliminated, chronic nonresponders dropped, and multiple content areas (SOGI, WFH, collaboration, management) removed in 2025 |
| **Statutory Context** | No Known Issue | Explicit statutory authority (13 U.S.C. 8(b), 131, 182; 42 U.S.C. 1861–76; COMPETES 2010), no substitute data source, required for GDP/SBA/MBDA program implementation |
| **Staffing and Funding** | High Risk | Census leadership removed (Santos → Cook), ~10–15% Census staff loss, NCSES FY26 budget request −40%, NSF staffing down ~one-third |
| **Policy** | High Risk | EO 14168-driven removal of SOGI questions plus other administration-priority content cuts, documented in the March 31, 2025 Federal Register notice |

**Overall risk picture:** The ABS is in little danger of disappearing — it is statutorily authorized, mandatory, actively fielded, and indispensable to GDP and federal small-business programs, and its historical archive is intact. The acute risks are to **what it measures and how well**: policy-driven content elimination, a materially reduced sample with weakened follow-up, and severe staffing/funding stress at both parent agencies that could degrade timeliness and quality in future cycles. Preservationists should prioritize archiving the 2021–2022 SOGI-related ABS tables (the only federal data on LGBTQ-owned employer businesses ever collected) and the pre-merger BERD series; data users should expect reduced off-cycle geographic/industry detail and a comparability break at the 2025/2026 redesign.
